extracted.intended_audience: story-tellers for children (parents, teachers, librarians, settlement workers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and sequencing short story programs for children over a year, focusing on psychological appeals, attention span, and curricular themes. Guidance covers how many stories per program, the order and function of each story, and thematic sequencing through the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of stories per program
rubrics_metrics.description: Three stories have been grouped in each program as the number upon which children can most easily fix their attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use three stories per session because this is the number children can most easily hold in attention. This is an explicit design choice tied to children's attention span.

rubrics_metrics.name: First story: apperceptive appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The first story in a group is an apperceptive one; it secures the child's spontaneous attention because, through its plot, it touches his own life in some way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a story that 'brings him into close and intimate touch with the interest theme of the program' by speaking of things the child knows and can do. Its purpose is immediate, spontaneous engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second story: appeals to reasoning / constructive thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The second story in each group makes an appeal to the child's reasoning powers; having secured his attention through the apperceptive story, the story-teller now takes the child a-field, mentally, and secures his voluntary attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a story that 'calls for constructive thought; it presents the theme of the program in a broader way, with wider application.' It is usually the longest story of the program and aims to develop reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third story: dessert — brevity and relaxation
rubrics_metrics.description: The third story is, invariably, the dessert of this story meal. Through its brevity, humor, tenderness, or sharply contrasting treatment of the program theme, it supplies the necessary relaxation, the fitting climax for the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End the program with a short piece that relaxes and completes the emotional arc — humorous, tender, or a contrast in form from the earlier stories to provide closure and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group by similar theme with contrasting form
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of similar theme, but contrasting form told in the story-hour have a mental effect of concentration and will training; the effect of one story of distinctly differentiated theme from one which has just been told is to break continuity of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within a program, keep the thematic thread consistent while varying form (tone, genre, length) to deepen focus and foster discipline; avoid abrupt theme changes that disrupt continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use instinctive and universal interests as program themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinctive and universal interests of all children form the themes of the story programs; these interests are presented in their natural order for a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select themes grounded in universal child interests (e.g., home, play, family) as the organizing principle for programs so stories resonate naturally with children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence themes in a yearly, natural order
rubrics_metrics.description: Themes are presented in their natural order for a year, beginning with home life, taking the child out into the world, and carrying him through his school, industrial, seasonable, and holiday activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan program progression across the year: start with home, then world/exploration, school, trade/industrial life, seasons, and holidays — matching stories to children's lived experiences over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological aim: promote definite mental growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan of grouping the stories in each program is very definite and psychologic. The book's aim is mental growth through stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and order stories with explicit educational/psychological goals (concentration, reasoning, will training), not merely entertainment. Each selection should contribute to child development objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical acceptance: stories may be told separately
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not intended that the stories shall never be told to children separately; on the contrary, each story is one of the best examples to be found of the child interest which forms its theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although organized into programs for educational effect, individual stories remain valuable in isolation; be flexible in use depending on context and audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and program analyses to illustrate choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses (e.g., the Trade Life program) illustrate the psychologic appeal upon which the book is built by mapping the apperceptive, reasoning, and dessert roles to concrete story selections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing programs, model them on worked examples: pair a concrete apperceptive opening, a broader reasoning middle (often a longer piece), and a short closing piece; the Preface uses 'The Holiday', 'Nils and the Bear', and 'The Giant Energy and Fairy Skill' as an explicit example.
